items.memo:
BILL NUMBER: S1476

SPONSOR: HOYLMAN
 
TITLE OF BILL:

An act to direct the department of financial services to study, evaluate
and make recommendations concerning lending practices by financial
institutions to landlords acquiring property that includes small busi-
ness tenants and/or rent-regulated tenants

 
SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:

Section 1 establishes legislation findings and intent to understand the
lender's role in "predatory equity", a practice which is furthering the
state's affordable housing crisis and displacement of commercial
tenants, who are mostly small business owners.

Section 2 defines financial institutions and small businesses and
directs the department of financial service (DFS) to prepare or have
prepared a study to review the process in which financial institutions
provide loans to landlords acquiring property that includes rent-regu-
lated and/or small business tenants. The section provides a list of
criteria for DFS to examine.

Section 3 authorizes the superintendent of DFS to draft and issue a
request for proposal to an outside firm to conduct the study.

Section 4 authorizes DFS to charge financial institutions for the costs
of conducting the study up to $350,000.

Section 5 establishes when DFS must report its findings to the governor
and the legislature.

Section 6 establishes when this act shall take effect.

 
JUSTIFICATION:

Over the past decade, the practice of predatory equity has destabilized
the affordable housing market and rent-regulation in New York City.
Between 2003 and 2007, Association for Neighborhood & Housing Develop-
ment research found that private equity-backed developers purchased an
estimated 100,000 units of affordable rent-regulated housing - nearly
10t of that housing stock. This number has only gone up in recent years.

Predatory equity is similar to subprime lending, which lead to the 2008
financial crisis and millions of foreclosures across the United States.
The practice involves landlords acquiring property that has very low to
moderate-income tenants in rent-regulated apartments, with highly specu-
lative loans. Aggressive landlords then engage in tenant harassment,
tack on illegal fees, and exploit poor physical conditions to displace
the tenants and return the apartments to market value. The methods are
often extreme. For example, one property owner tried by the New York
Attorney General for unlawful eviction of rent stabilized tenants,
embarked on a campaign to get rid of rent-stabilized tenants including
cutting off the heat and repeatedly exposing the tenants to lead dust.
As a result, tenants testified that they used ovens to heat their apart-
ments, bathed using buckets and constantly held their noses and mouths
to protect against the lead dust.

Predatory equity is a significant problem that severely exacerbates the
affordability crisis, which has already reached a fever pitch throughout
New York. Many landlords have been exposed for engaging in this practice
but the banks, that have eluded any responsibility, are equally to
blame. It appears that there are few underwriting standards and specula-
tors are able to easily secure a mortgage to cover up to 80% of the
acquisition costs of a piece of property. Due to the ensuing debt obli-
gations landlords then must engage in systematic harassment and other
means to replace all low-income paying tenants with higher paying resi-
dents.

Not only rent regulated tenants are impacted, small businesses are as
well. In case after case, landlords push out local businesses in order
to hold out for luxury retail or corporate chains capable of paying
higher rents. The result is a glut of empty storefronts, chain stores,
pharmacies, and high-end national brands that often lack local character
and don't provide goods and services the community needs.

There is a complete lack of transparency in regards to the practices and
standards the financial institutions follow when making the types of
loans involved in predatory equity. Therefore, it is necessary that the
Department of Financial Services is authorized to issue a Request for
Proposal (RFP) to an outside entity to conduct a robust study on the
practice of predatory equity. Once the full scope of the problem is
fully understood the appropriate steps may be taken to eliminate this
heinous practice.

 
PRIOR LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

2018: S.8675-A (Hoylman) - Died in Banks

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
This act shall take effect immediately.
